hints: Look at the neutralisation equation and notice the 1 to 1 link, one $H^+$ needs exactly one $OH^-$.
Start by finding moles of $H^+$ in the big tank using moles = concentration x volume with $1.26 \times 10^{-3}$ and $11000$.
Convert those moles of $NaOH$ to mass using $M_r = 40.0$, and watch out for using just $OH^-$ instead of the whole solid.
walkthrough:
**Find the mole ratio**

Think simply, each $H^+$ is mopped up by one $OH^-$ to make water. So moles of $NaOH$ needed equals moles of $H^+$ present.

$$H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O \text{, ratio 1 : 1}$$

**Calculate moles of acid**

Use the golden rule, moles = concentration x volume. Do not be put off by the huge volume.

$$n(H^+) = [H^+] \times V = (1.26 \times 10^{-3}) \times 11000 = 13.86 \text{ mol}$$

**Convert to mass of NaOH**

You need the same 13.86 mol of $NaOH$. The $M_r$ of $NaOH$ is $23.0 + 16.0 + 1.0 = 40.0$.

$$m = n \times M_r = 13.86 \times 40.0 = 554.4 \text{ g}$$

**Choose the answer**

That rounds to about 554 g, which neutralises all the acid in the sample.

options.A: Far too small. This ignores the huge $11000 \text{ dm}^3$ volume and involves a power-of-ten error. Always multiply concentration by the full given volume.
options.B: This is the mass for only $1 \text{ dm}^3$: $(1.26 \times 10^{-3}) \times 40.0 = 0.0504 \text{ g}$. The trap is forgetting to multiply by 11000 for the real sample.
options.C: This uses $M_r = 17$ for $OH^-$ only: $13.86 \times 17 = 236 \text{ g}$. But you weigh out solid $NaOH$, so you must use $M_r = 40.0$ including $Na^+$.
options.D: Correct and well done. Moles $H^+ = 13.86$ mol, so moles $NaOH = 13.86$ mol, mass $= 13.86 \times 40.0 = 554$ g.
